strengths: The paper identifies a clearly motivated and practically relevant problem: knowledge distillation under covariate shift where the student relies on spurious features for groups entirely absent from the training data. The teacher-student disagreement signal is an elegant, label-free way to localize student biases without requiring knowledge of which features are spurious.

ConfiG is well-motivated technically: maximizing the nonlinearly transformed confidence gap between teacher and student in the latent space of Stable Diffusion (via null-text inversion) preserves the causal/class-relevant feature while suppressing student shortcuts. The qualitative examples (Figs. 3, 4, 6-8) convincingly demonstrate that ConfiG removes spurious attributes while baselines do not.

Comprehensive and well-designed experiments: three datasets (CelebA, SpuCo Birds, Spurious ImageNet), multiple students (ViT-T, ViT-S, TinyViT, ResNet-18), consistent gains over strong diffusion-based augmentation baselines (DAFusion, DistDiff, GIF, ActGen), and a full factorial-style analysis of augmentation type (CutMix/MixUp/etc.) x synthetic augmentation x EDRM (Tables 4, 12, 13). The finding that 2x high-quality augmentations beat 5-10x baseline augmentations (Table 8) is a valuable insight.

A theoretical contribution (Prop. 1, Lemma 1 in App. A.1) formally shows that augmentations from a set where the teacher is confident and the student is not provably decrease the generalization gap term Omega, connecting the empirical observations to a principled decomposition. Assumptions are discussed and are reasonable.

Thorough ablations: number of augmentations, combining with TAB, ERM+EDRM interaction, cost analysis (App. A.7), hyperparameter details, and honest reporting of cases where ConfiG is only second-best (Spurious mAUC on ImageNet vs. DAFusion).

The limitations section is candid and substantive: the method requires a robust teacher and inherits that teacher's robustness ceiling; the CelebA student nearly saturates the teacher's worst-group accuracy, showing both the strength and the ceiling of the approach.
weaknesses: Dependence on an artificially strong teacher weakens practical significance: on SpuCo Birds the teacher is a ViT-B fine-tuned on the full balanced training set (i.e., the method's supporting teacher has access to data the student never sees), and on ImageNet the teacher checkpoint is from VanillaKD's own setup. The paper's central claim is about groups 'unknowingly absent' from training data, but obtaining a teacher that is robust on exactly those absent groups is itself nontrivial and only briefly acknowledged in the limitations.

Scalability and cost of the method are underexplored: per-image null-text inversion plus stochastic latent optimization (11.4 s/image) with a two-stage pipeline (auxiliary student, then final student) may limit applicability beyond small-scale training sets (500-2500 images in the main experiments). Only ImageNet-100-subset experiments go beyond the curated small-scale setting, and there the gain on the primary spurious metric is only second-best with a modest margin.

The spurious features in CelebA and SpuCo Birds are deliberately engineered to be simple, well-defined binary attributes (hair color, glasses, background). It is unclear how well the confidence-gap guidance behaves for complex, entangled, or unknown biases where teacher-student disagreement may not localize cleanly onto a removable spurious feature; the eye-color observation in Sec. 4.2 hints at this but is not studied systematically.

The theoretical result is somewhat orthogonal to the actual algorithm: Proposition 1 shows improvement for augmentations drawn from an idealized support defined via confidence thresholds (Eq. 13), but does not establish that the diffusion-optimization procedure (Eq. 7) actually samples from, or near, that support, and epsilon_aug is assumed rather than controlled.

Some clarity issues: Figure 2's evidence that disagreement indicates spurious-feature reliance is correlational; the choice of gamma=2 for the confidence transforms is empirical with limited sensitivity analysis; the fairness implications of gender classification on CelebA are not discussed despite being a sensitive task, even though a societal-impact discussion could easily have been included and would have strengthened the paper.
No explicit statement about code release, which, given the multi-stage pipeline and many implementation details (5 optimization steps, prompts, etc.), affects reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: knowledge distillation under covariate shift where spurious features are present in training but absent at test time, and where the groups are 'unknowingly absent'. The teacher-student disagreement signal is an elegant way to target student-specific shortcuts without requiring explicit annotation of spurious features.

The proposed method (ConfIG) is clearly described, builds sensibly on null-text inversion and guided diffusion, and is well differentiated from prior diffusion-based augmentation baselines (DistDiff, DAFusion, GIF, ActGen), which are student-agnostic or lack explicit teacher-student guidance.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: three datasets (CelebA, SpuCo Birds, Spurious ImageNet), multiple metrics (worst-group, group-mean, sample-mean, spuIN mAUC), multiple student architectures (ViT-T, ViT-S, TinyViT, ResNet-18), ablations on augmentation count, combinations with TAB, cost/quality analysis, and full results in the appendix. Consistent improvements in worst-group accuracy are notable (e.g., 66.1% vs 38.9% CutMix on CelebA).

The paper includes a theoretical decomposition of the generalization error and a proposition showing under which conditions confidence-guided augmentations provably decrease |Ω|, connecting the method to the empirical observations, and honestly discusses a genuine limitation: the requirement of a robust teacher.

Qualitative analysis is convincing: augmented samples meaningfully increase student loss and decrease student accuracy while preserving teacher confidence, and the method even uncovered an unanticipated spurious correlation (eye color), supporting the 'unknown bias' claim.
weaknesses: The setup relies on a strong circularity: the method requires a teacher that is robust to the very covariate shift the student must handle, yet obtaining such a teacher presupposes access to balanced data (a fine-tuned ViT-B on the full balanced SpuCo Birds) or a CLIP model that is already robust for other reasons. In the SpuCo Birds case the paper itself acknowledges that CLIP's poor worst-group performance forced them to fine-tune a teacher on a balanced dataset — which substantially weakens the practical relevance of the 'unknown covariate shift' setting, since a balanced dataset with the missing groups would already be available.

The empirical gains over the strongest baseline (ActGen with CutMix+EDRM) are moderate in several settings (e.g., 80.7 vs 80.2 group mean on SpuCo Birds; 93.3 vs 93.3/93.2 validation accuracy and only ~0.5–1 mAUC gains on Spurious ImageNet), so the headline improvements rest mostly on worst-group CelebA results with deliberately injected spurious correlations.

The covariate shift is artificially constructed by subsampling known attributes (blond/young females, glasses, background), so the spurious features are known to the experimenters a priori even if not to the method; this limits how strongly the results support robustness to genuinely unknown distribution shift.

The theoretical result (Proposition 1) relies on strong and largely unverifiable assumptions (uniform approximation of p* by the teacher within δ_t on the union of supports, student-teacher gap δ_s on train support, and a support condition defining Q), so it provides intuition rather than a practically checkable guarantee.

ConfIG is computationally expensive (11.4 s/image for latent optimization, roughly 5x baselines), and the mitigation argument (better quality at 2x than baselines at 10x) is dataset- and metric-specific; scalability to realistic dataset sizes with many classes (the ImageNet subset uses 100 classes and 250 images/class) is not demonstrated.

Hyperparameter/model selection uses a validation split containing only groups present in training, which is reasonable under the stated assumption but means the method's behavior when even the validation distribution shifts is unexplored.

Some writing issues remain (e.g., Figure 4 caption 'changes removes', 'traning data' typos in appendix figures), and the reliance on Stable Diffusion 1.4 as implicit teacher for all baselines raises questions about whether ConfIG's gains partly stem from better use of a shared generator rather than the confidence-guidance idea itself — though the ActGen comparison partially addresses this.

strengths: Motivating and well-posed problem: distillation from robust teachers under covariate shift where spurious groups are entirely absent from training data. The diagnostic in Figure 2 (teacher-student disagreement on absent groups) is a clean, convincing motivating observation.

The proposed method (ConfiG) is technically elegant: maximizing teacher-student confidence disagreement in a guided diffusion framework directly targets the student's shortcuts without requiring explicit knowledge of the spurious features. Figure 3 clearly contrasts this with prior student-agnostic augmentation baselines.

Strong and comprehensive empirical evidence: consistent gains across worst-group, group-mean, and sample-mean accuracy on CelebA, SpuCo Birds, and spurious ImageNet (mAuC), with comparisons against four diffusion-based augmentation baselines and standard augmentation baselines, and 3-seed standard deviations reported.

Thorough ablations: number of augmentations (2x is optimal), quality vs. quantity analysis (Table 8 shows baselines underperform even with 5-10x more data), multiple student architectures (TinyViT, ResNet-18, ViT-S), larger training set (Table 7), and combination with TAB. Table 2's analysis of student accuracy/loss on augmented samples provides useful mechanistic insight.

The appendix includes a theoretical proposition (with proof) that confidence-guided augmentations provably reduce the covariate-shift generalization gap under clearly stated, plausibly realistic assumptions, and the paper discusses when the conditions hold in practice.

Limits of the method are honestly discussed in the limitations section (need for a suitably robust teacher, and the SpuCo Birds teacher requiring a balanced fine-tuning set), and computational cost is quantified (A.7).

Table 4 demonstrates the method is agnostic to the base augmentation scheme (improves MixUp, AutoAugment, CutMixPick as well), and the qualitative results including the serendipitous discovery of an unintended eye-color bias (Sec. 4.2) support the claim of identifying unknown spurious correlations.
weaknesses: The 'robust teacher' assumption is a substantial practical bottleneck, partially acknowledged: on SpuCo Birds the teacher was fine-tuned on the full balanced training set, which arguably undercuts the limited-data narrative for that benchmark. The method's value depends on availability of teachers that are robust on the very groups the pipeline aims to handle.

Gains on Spurious ImageNet are comparatively modest (second-best validation accuracy behind DAFusion; spurious mAuC advantage of at least 0.5%), so the evidence for the non-group-shift setting is less convincing than for the group-shift benchmarks, which are somewhat artificial (groups deliberately removed).

The method requires a separate auxiliary student distilled only on real images plus per-image null-text inversion and stochastic latent optimization (11.4 s/image vs 2-3 s for baselines). While A.5/A.7 argue quality outweighs quantity, the multi-stage pipeline (auxiliary student + guided generation + final distillation) adds complexity that is not fully reflected in the headline comparison.

The theoretical result is essentially a consistency argument resting on strong assumptions (teacher approximates p* uniformly on train/test/augmented support; student matches teacher on train support; epsilon_aug controllability). The connection between the empirical objective in Eq. 7 and the assumed support definition in Eq. 13 (simultaneous student confidence below and teacher above thresholds) is heuristic rather than enforced by the optimizer.
Only 3 random seeds per experiment; for worst-group accuracy with large variances in some baselines (e.g., CutMixPick ±13.1), the significance of some comparisons is unclear.

Societal considerations are thin: gender classification on CelebA is a known sensitive task with fairness implications, and the method intentionally generates synthetic faces (including faces of real individuals via inversion); a discussion of consent, misuse, and demographic representativeness of the augmentation strategy would strengthen the paper.

Scalability beyond small curated benchmarks is untested: experiments use 500-25,000 training images; it remains unclear whether disagreement-based guidance scales to full ImageNet-scale distillation where spurious correlations are subtler and more numerous.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: knowledge distillation under covariate shift with spurious features, supported by an empirical motivating analysis (Fig. 2, Tab. 1) showing teacher-student disagreement concentrates on groups absent from training data.

ConfiG is a sensible and clearly described method: inter-class mixing as warm-start plus latent optimization that maximizes teacher-student disagreement, built on the established DiG-IN/null-text inversion framework.

Extensive and largely fair empirical evaluation: six strong diffusion-augmentation baselines, compute-matched comparison via FLOPs multipliers (App. C), six training runs with std. on group shift datasets, and many ablations (components, stronger standard augmentations, augmentation count, weaker teachers, different architectures, replacement probability).

Honest reporting: on BAR the method is not always best; App. K shows the advantage narrows with larger, less biased training data; App. L shows baselines beat ConfiG 1x in the no-covariate-shift 5-shot setting; failure cases are analyzed (App. O).

A theoretical proposition (App. A) formalizes the intuition that augmentations more challenging for the student than the teacher reduce the covariate-shift gap |Omega|, with a candid discussion of its practical limitations.
Meaningful limitations section (classification-only, requires strong pre-trained teacher, augmentations applied globally).
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is modest: Proposition 1 is a fairly direct risk-decomposition under strong, unverifiable assumptions (teacher KL bounded on all supports, augmented data more challenging for student, etc.), and the authors themselves concede the constants are inestimable in practice; it functions as motivation rather than a predictive theory.

The method inherits a strong implicit assumption that the teacher (e.g., CLIP zero-shot) is itself robust on unseen covariate groups; for domains where CLIP/SD coverage is poor, the approach may degrade, and sensitivity to this assumption is only partially explored (weaker-teacher ablation covers two datasets).

ConfiG relies on a cascade of existing techniques (DiG-IN, null-text inversion, prompt-to-prompt, Diff-Mix-style inter-class mixing); novelty is primarily in the disagreement-driven objective and its combination, which some may view as incremental.
Per-image optimization cost is ~10-70x that of some baselines; while FLOPs are matched, wall-clock cost and practicality of one-auxiliary-student-per-setup plus rejection sampling are nontrivial.

Gains are dataset-dependent: improvements on BAR are inconsistent (second-best behind Diff-Mix in Tab. 2), and non-synthetic augmentations (MixUp/AutoAugment) alone can surpass synthetic-only results on BAR; ImageNet-100 student trainings are performed only once, so reported improvements (~1.6%) carry no variance estimate.

CelebA-HQ evaluation uses a custom train/test swap with highly imbalanced groups (Fig. 6: 74 to 11755 images per group), which makes WGA noisy and complicates comparison to prior spurious-correlation literature.

strengths: The core idea — guiding diffusion-based augmentation by maximizing teacher-student disagreement under covariate shift — is well-motivated and clearly differentiated from prior model-agnostic diffusion augmentation methods (GIF, DistDiff, DA-Fusion, Diff-Mix, Diff-II, ActGen), with the closest baseline (ActGen) explicitly discussed and empirically distinguished.

The empirical evidence is extensive and carefully designed: six diffusion-augmentation baselines, four datasets, FLOP-matched generation budgets, six training repetitions with standard deviations, and a large set of ablations (component-wise, augmentation count, replacement probability, stronger non-synthetic augmentations, weaker teachers, alternative teacher/student architectures, single-step diffusion backbone, failure cases).

The improvements on worst-group and mean-group accuracy (e.g., WGA 88.15 vs. 75.68 for the best baseline on CelebA-HQ) are substantial and directly support the paper's central claim about mitigating shortcut learning from unseen groups.

The decomposition of the generalization error into Ψ and Ω terms, plus the empirical motivation in Fig. 2/Table 1 (disagreement concentrates on absent groups), provides a coherent conceptual framing; the appendix proposition, while heavily assumption-laden, is honestly caveated by the authors themselves.

Limitations and failure modes (BAR inconsistencies, out-of-distribution generations, resolution limits for localization tasks, dependence on strong pre-trained teachers) are discussed candidly, which strengthens the scientific case.
weaknesses: ConfiG is by far the most expensive method per augmentation (Tab. 11), and the FLOP-matching comparison relies on an estimated backward-pass factor of 2 with acknowledged uncertainty; if the true cost is higher, the reported advantage over baselines shrinks. The method's practicality relative to cheaper baselines like Diff-Mix therefore remains questionable.

The gains on the headline metric (sample mean accuracy) are often marginal or second-best only, e.g., BAR where Diff-Mix wins SMA and stronger standard augmentations alone can rival synthetic augmentation; the most convincing wins are confined to WGA/GMA on CelebA-HQ and SpuCo Birds.

The theoretical proposition is essentially a restatement of the method's intuition under restrictive assumptions (bounded KL, support conditions on Q, constants Θ, Δp, α) that the authors admit are infeasible to estimate in practice; it adds limited falsifiable insight beyond the empirical motivation.

The CelebA-HQ protocol (training on the original test split, evaluating on the train split) is unconventional; while justified, it limits comparability with prior work on this dataset and deserves stronger validation that conclusions transfer to standard splits.

The empirical claim that teacher-student disagreement is a reliable proxy for group membership is established only on synthetic, deliberately constructed biases (binary spurious features); whether the method generalizes to natural, non-categorical, or unknown spurious correlations is not demonstrated, and the ImageNet-100 experiments (single run, SpuScore metric) only partially address this.

Overall, the contribution is a competent, well-engineered combination of existing components (null-text inversion, prompt-to-prompt editing, DiG-IN guidance, inter-class mixing from Diff-Mix) rather than a fundamentally new technique, which caps its significance for an Algorithms/General contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a clearly important and underexplored problem: knowledge distillation when unseen groups are fully absent from the training data, where existing diffusion-based augmentation baselines (which only manipulate existing samples) cannot target the student's spurious features.

The core idea of ConfiG is elegant and well-motivated: maximizing teacher-student disagreement while preserving teacher confidence identifies regions where the student relies on shortcuts, without requiring any explicit knowledge of what the biases are. The empirical motivation (Fig. 2, Tab. 1 showing 94-96% of disagreements occur on absent groups) convincingly supports the premise.

Extensive and fair experimental evaluation: six state-of-the-art diffusion-based augmentation baselines, computational cost matched in FLOPs (App. C), four datasets covering both group shift and class-level spurious features, six training runs with standard deviations, and consistent improvements especially in WGA/GMA (e.g., +34% WGA on CelebA-HQ over real data).

Thorough ablation studies: component-wise analysis (Tab. 4), stronger standard augmentations (Tab. 5), scaling of augmentations (Tab. 6, Fig. 8), weaker teachers (Tab. 7, 22), different architectures (Tab. 18), replacement probabilities (Tab. 19-20), and compatibility with modern single-step diffusion models (App. E). The comparison with model-centric bias mitigation methods (Tab. 8) is a valuable addition showing complementarity.

A formal theoretical treatment (Proposition 1, Lemma 1) motivates why student-challenging augmentations reduce the generalization gap |Ω|, with an honest discussion of when the assumptions hold and their practical limitations (App. A).

The paper is well written and clearly structured, with detailed hyperparameters (App. B) supporting reproducibility, a qualitative analysis including failure cases (App. O), and a meaningful limitations and future work section.

Notable honest reporting: the paper acknowledges cases where ConfiG does not dominate (BAR SMA in Tab. 2, weaker teacher settings, performance drop without covariate shift in App. L), which strengthens credibility.
weaknesses: The central assumption that a robust, well-calibrated teacher (e.g., CLIP) exists that approximates p* on both train and test distributions is strong. The method essentially transfers the coverage problem to the foundation model; if the teacher or diffusion model itself lacks coverage of the unseen groups, ConfiG cannot help. The weaker-teacher ablation partially addresses this, but a deeper discussion of when this assumption fails (e.g., domain-specific applications without general-purpose teachers) would strengthen the work.

The optimization objective (Eq. 7) targets teacher-student disagreement for a randomly sampled target class. It is not guaranteed that the resulting samples specifically populate the covariate-shift regions relevant to the true test distribution; the method may also generate hard-but-informative samples unrelated to spurious correlations. The theory assumes p* is concentrated around teacher predictions on supp(Q) (Eq. 37), which is exactly the point in question and only argued, not verified empirically.

The theoretical contribution, while a nice motivation, is relatively straightforward (a risk decomposition plus worst-case bounds under idealized assumptions), and the authors themselves concede the constants are inestimable in practice; the value is motivational rather than predictive.

Computational cost of ConfiG is roughly an order of magnitude higher per augmentation than the strongest baselines (App. C), and while FLOPs are matched, generation cost and latency remain a practical concern; the backward-pass FLOP factor of 2 is only an estimate.

Results on BAR are less consistent for ConfiG (second-best SMA in the main table, and failure cases acknowledged in App. O), and gains shrink considerably with larger, less-biased training sets (Tab. 23), suggesting the advantage is confined to the strongly biased, small-data regime the paper constructs itself.

ImageNet-100 experiments use only a single training run per method due to cost, making the reported ~1.6-1.8% improvements harder to interpret against run-to-run variance, and the CelebA-HQ setting (training data drawn from the original test split, evaluation on the train split) is non-standard and requires careful justification beyond pre-training separation.

The comparison framing could be more precise: most baselines were not designed for group robustness under fully absent groups, so the consistent WGA gains, while impressive, partly reflect a favorable task selection; comparisons against group-robustness methods combined with synthetic data would contextualize the contribution further.
